ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study involves human participants and was approved by Newcastle University, the Mbeya College of Health Sciences Institutional Review Board, and the Tanzanian National Research Ethics Committee.
6 Eligible participants were aged 60 years or older, resident in one of the three study communities, and consented to participate.
All participants gave informed consent following a village information meeting and subsequent verbal and written information.

Multidimensional deprivation was measured using a Multidimensional Deprivation Index constructed with the Alkire-Foster counting methodology. 28 This framework is the most widely used and internationally recognised approach to multidimensional poverty measurement and underpins the global Multidimensional Poverty Index. 1, 8 The method identifies individuals experiencing overlapping deprivations across multiple domains of wellbeing. 29 Participants were assessed against a set of nine predefined indicators, each with a deprivation cutoff, and classified as deprived or not deprived on each.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction Dementia and late-life depression are rising rapidly in sub-Saharan Africa, yet prevention frameworks remain focused on individual behaviour.
Multidimensional poverty is a plausible structural determinant of brain health but is rarely assessed.
aged 60 years and older in three rural communities in Kilimanjaro, Tanzania.
Outcomes were the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), IDEA cognitive screen, CERAD ten-word list, and verbal fluency.
Deprivation was measured with a nine-indicator Alkire-Foster Multidimensional Deprivation Index.
Missing data were multiply imputed; models adjusted for age, sex, education, community, comorbidity, and health behaviours.
Of 1054 participants (mean age 70.2 years [SD 9.35]; 629 [59.7%] women), 840 (81.9%) of 1026 were multidimensionally deprived.

Each unit increase in deprivation score predicted a higher GDS-15 score (β 4.83, 95% CI 3.82 to 5.83), higher odds of screen-positive depression (odds ratio 17.18, 6.89 to 42.83), lower IDEA score (β -1.97, -2.97 to -0.97), and lower verbal fluency (β -2.57, -3.77 to -1.36; all p<0.001).

text.text: CERAD measures and self-reported impairment showed no association.
At community level this gradient inverted: the most deprived community had the lowest depression and highest cognition, yet perceived social standing did not differ.
Multidimensional deprivation was near-universal and independently associated with worse brain health.

The community-level inversion, with perceived social standing equivalent across communities of unequal material circumstances, indicates that absolute deprivation alone does not explain the distribution of brain health.
Relative position and community resilience are priorities for study.
Brain health in later life, encompassing cognitive function and mental wellbeing, is a growing global priority.

Cognitive decline spans a spectrum from mild impairment to dementia, 16 while depression is characterised by persistent low mood, loss of interest, and impaired daily functioning. 17 Both carry substantial consequences for independence, quality of life, and mortality, share common risk factors, frequently co-occur, and may be bidirectionally related. 18, 19 The burden is shifting decisively toward the global south, and eastern sub-Saharan Africa is projected to experience one of the steepest increases in dementia cases worldwide by 2050. 20 In the Hai district studied here, dementia prevalence in adults aged 70 years and older rose from 6.4% in 2009-2010 to 8.9% in 2018-2019. 27 Prevention frameworks have so far concentrated on individually modifiable risk.

text.text: The 2024 Lancet Commission identified 14 modifiable risk factors accounting for approximately 45% of dementia cases worldwide. 23 Recent work argues that this framework under-represents the realities of the global south, 21, 22 and shows that incorporating poverty, wealth shocks, income inequality, and HIV raises the potentially preventable fraction to as much as 65%. 24 There are corresponding calls to shift prevention from individually targeted behaviour change toward structural approaches, since behaviour-based prevention places the burden on individuals and may widen disparities when better-resourced groups benefit disproportionately. 25, 26 Poverty is among the most consequential of these structural determinants, and is increasingly understood as multidimensional rather than purely economic. 1 Individuals commonly experience overlapping social, material, and psychosocial deprivations that interact to shape health. 1, 2 This is reflected in the global Multidimensional Poverty Index adopted by the United Nations Development Programme, which assesses deprivation across health, education, and standard of living and classifies individuals as multidimensionally poor when they experience a weighted threshold of deprivations. 8, 9 Income-based measures alone capture neither the lived experience of poverty nor its consequences, whereas multidimensional measures help identify priority areas for intervention. 7 Older adults are particularly exposed.

text.text: This study assessed multidimensional deprivation in older adults in the Kilimanjaro region of northern Tanzania and examined its associations with depressive symptoms and cognitive function.
By identifying which dimensions of deprivation carry the greatest association with each outcome, we aimed to inform the design of targeted, multisectoral interventions.
We conducted a cross-sectional analysis using data from the Akili Mali (Brain Wealth) study, a community-based study of older adults in the Hai district of Kilimanjaro region, northern Tanzania.
Hai is a rural district on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, with a population of 240 999 at the 2022 national census, 79.3% of whom live in rural areas.

The majority of older residents are subsistence farmers and levels of illiteracy in this age group are high, reflecting historically limited access to schooling. 14 Dementia prevalence in this population rose over the decade to 2019, against declines reported in several high-income settings. 27 The study includes three rural communities stratified by geography and socioeconomic status, selected by the District Medical Office as typical exemplars of these strata: Narumu Tella, a highland community of relatively higher socioeconomic status; Orori, a neighbouring highland community of relatively lower socioeconomic status; and Sanya Station, a geographically and culturally distinct lowland community.

text.text: A door-to-door census was conducted in each community by balozis, elected leaders of ten households who report to the village committee, recording year of birth and sex of all residents.

Individuals born in 1965 or earlier were eligible, assuming a January birth date, and all were invited through door-to-door information delivered by members of the Akili Mali Lay Advisory Board, older residents of the participating communities who advise the study and are co-authors of this paper, together with the village committee.
Those too frail to attend a study centre were offered a home visit, and those too unwell to participate were excluded and referred to services.
6 Eligible participants were aged 60 years or older, resident in one of the three study communities, and consented to participate.
Where data were implausible, field teams returned to verify and correct entries, and years of birth were revised accordingly.
All residents identified by the census as born in 1965 or earlier were invited to take part, and 1054 were confirmed as aged 60 years or older on verification of year of birth.
Year of birth was not known for 13 participants, whose age is therefore an estimate.
All participants gave informed consent following a village information meeting and subsequent verbal and written information.
For participants unable to read, information was read aloud by a study team member and consent was indicated using a thumbprint.
Those lacking capacity to consent were included only with evidence of active willingness to participate and with consent provided by a close relative.

Multidimensional deprivation was measured using a Multidimensional Deprivation Index constructed with the Alkire-Foster counting methodology. 28 This framework is the most widely used and internationally recognised approach to multidimensional poverty measurement and underpins the global Multidimensional Poverty Index. 1, 8 The method identifies individuals experiencing overlapping deprivations across multiple domains of wellbeing. 29 Participants were assessed against a set of nine predefined indicators, each with a deprivation cutoff, and classified as deprived or not deprived on each.

text.text: Indicators were coded in binary form (1 = deprived,0 = not deprived) and summed to give a deprivation count from 0 to 9.
A normalised index score was computed as the mean of all binary indicators, producing a continuous measure between 0 and 1.

Participants deprived on three or more indicators were 7 classified as multidimensionally deprived, following the convention adopted in the global index for a nine-indicator specification. 8, 28 Those with fewer than six valid indicators were not assigned a binary classification.

text.text: The dimensions used align with the global Multidimensional Poverty Index domains of education, health, and living standards. 8 Indicator selection was informed by the global index to facilitate comparison, while being adapted to reflect local context and available data.

text.text: Within the education dimension, years of schooling and literacy capture formal attainment and current functional capability, respectively.
We used an individual-level adaptation of the global index threshold of six years of schooling, and substituted literacy for school attendance to suit an older population.

Within the health dimension, food insecurity and dietary diversity reflect short-term and structural aspects of food deprivation, both associated with adverse mental health and cognitive outcomes in later life. 30 The global index uses body-mass index to indicate undernutrition, but that measure has important limitations in older populations.

text.text: Living standards were assessed with five indicators.

Solid cooking fuel use and inadequate housing materials follow established global index cutoffs; household air pollution from solid fuel combustion remains one of the leading environmental risk factors globally and is concentrated in low-income settings. 31 Household crowding captures constrained living space, and absence of glass windows was used as a further marker of housing quality.

text.text: Low perceived safety, although not a standard global index indicator, was included because perceived safety influences mobility, social participation, and mental health in older adults. 32 It was defined as a score at or below the sample 25th centile, a value of 7.0 or lower on the 1 to 10 scale, because the distribution was heavily skewed toward feeling safe.

text.text: The full indicator set with cutoffs, derivation and source is given in online supplemental appendix 1.
Cognition was assessed using instruments with prior validation and normative data for Tanzania.
The Identification and Intervention for Dementia in Elderly Africans (IDEA) cognitive screen total score measured general cognition.

It was developed for populations with low levels of formal education and, across Nigerian and Tanzanian cohorts, showed area under the receiver operating characteristic curve above 0.9 in all settings and no evidence of educational bias. 33 Two components were additionally analysed as full-scale scores because normative data were available: the CERAD ten-word list learning task, with minor local adaptation, 34 and one-minute categorical verbal fluency using animal naming.

text.text: Depressive symptoms were assessed using a previously established Swahili translation of the 15item Geriatric Depression Scale. 35 Although the scale is designed for self-administration, high levels of illiteracy and uncorrected near vision impairment meant that for most participants it was administered by a clinical research assistant.

text.text: A score of 5 or more was classified as screenpositive depression.

At this cutoff, pooled sensitivity across 43 studies is 0.89 and pooled specificity 0.77. 36 Most sociodemographic and general health measures were obtained by selfreport, including history of stroke, diabetes, HIV and treated hypertension, with the exception of body-mass index and blood pressure, which were measured at assessment.

text.text: In this community-based study of 1054 older adults in rural northern Tanzania, multidimensional deprivation was the norm rather than the exception, with more than four in five participants meeting the threshold for multidimensional poverty.

Higher index scores predicted greater depressive symptom burden, markedly increased odds of screen-positive depression, and poorer performance on global cognitive screening and verbal fluency, after adjustment for age, sex, education, community, comorbidity, and health behaviours.

Three findings merit particular attention: the depression association strengthened rather than attenuated on adjustment; deprivation tracked measured cognition but bore no relationship to participants' own reports of difficulty; and the most deprived community had the best brain health outcomes, inverting the individual gradient.

The magnitude of the depression association is substantial, corresponding to an odds ratio of 1.37 for each additional deprivation and to a 17.2-fold difference in odds across the full range of the index after full adjustment.
That the association strengthened on adjustment requires explanation rather than dismissal.

Sanya Station combined the highest material deprivation with by far the lowest depression prevalence, so in unadjusted analysis this community-level pattern operated against the individual-level association and suppressed it; only when community entered the model did the underlying relationship emerge fully.

This is substantive rather than technical, because it shows that aggregate comparisons across communities can obscure, and even reverse, relationships operating within them, a caution directly relevant to how population-level deprivation data are read in low-resource settings.

That living standards deprivation was the strongest predictor of depressive symptoms, ahead of health and education, suggests that the immediate material conditions of daily life may bear more directly on mood in later life than educational history.
Our observed prevalence of screen-positive depression, at 69.3%, is high and warrants careful framing.

Prevalence estimates for late-life depression in sub-Saharan Africa vary by an order of magnitude according to ascertainment method, with the Geriatric Depression Scale consistently yielding higher pooled prevalence than structured diagnostic interviews. 15, 41 At the cutoff used here, pooled specificity of 0.77 implies that a meaningful proportion of those screening positive would not meet diagnostic criteria. 36 Regional comparison is instructive: in neighbouring Moshi district a community study using the same instrument reported depressive symptoms in 44.4%, 52 whereas in Hai district structured DSM-IV assessment yielded 21.2%. 53 Our figure should therefore be read as symptom burden captured by a screening instrument rather than the prevalence of major depressive disorder.

text.text: Associations with global cognitive screening and verbal fluency were robust to full adjustment, whereas those with CERAD list learning and delayed recall were not.

Verbal fluency draws on 20 lexical access, executive control, and processing speed, and may be a more sensitive marker of early or diffuse cognitive change than verbal learning and recall, which can show floor effects in populations with limited formal schooling.

That the memory associations attenuated specifically after adjustment for age, education, and community suggests these variables, rather than deprivation itself, account for the crude differences initially observed.

Education emerged as the dominant deprivation dimension for cognition, consistent with cognitive reserve theory. 42 This raises a methodological concern, since educational deprivation contributes to the index while years of education independently predicts cognitive test performance.

text.text: The most theoretically challenging finding is the inversion between material deprivation and brain health at community level.

Sanya Station was the most deprived community overall and on most individual indicators, yet had the lowest depression prevalence and the strongest cognitive performance, while Orori, intermediate in overall material deprivation, had the worst outcomes on most measures and performed significantly worse than its immediate highland neighbour Narumu Tella on both depression and cognition.

This pattern resists explanation through absolute material deprivation alone but is consistent with relative deprivation theory, which 21 holds that health is shaped not only by absolute resources but by an individual's standing relative to a salient reference group, with adverse comparison generating psychosocial stress. 43 Two pathways are conventionally proposed, one material and one psychosocial, the latter operating through chronic stress and cumulative allostatic load. 44 Our measure of perceived social standing bears directly on this reading: within the the village (Spearman r -0.35, p<0.001) and, more weakly, nationally (r -0.08, p=0.029), so the ladder does track measured deprivation at the individual level.

text.text: Across communities, however, perceived standing was statistically indistinguishable: village ladder means were 3.22 in Narumu Tella, 3.20 in Orori, and 3.31 in Sanya Station (p=0.78), and national ladder means were 3.94, 3.79, and 3.91 respectively (p=0.79), even though measured deprivation differed significantly between every pair of communities.

That older adults in the most materially deprived community rate their social position no lower than those in the least deprived is itself consistent with a relative rather than absolute standard of comparison: if people judge their position chiefly against neighbours rather than against the country, perceived standing will be approximately equalised even where objective circumstances diverge.

The salient comparison for Orori residents is Narumu Tella, an adjacent community selected precisely because it is better off, whereas Sanya Station is geographically and culturally distinct from both highland communities, so its residents' reference group is likely internal to a community in which deprivation is widely shared.

Sanya Station also differs in topography, natural resources and ethnic composition, being the only community with a substantial Maasai population, and these differences may bear on both outlook and assessment.

Language is the most immediate concern, since all instruments were administered in Swahili, but it does not appear to explain the pattern: confidence speaking Swahili did not differ across the three communities (96.3%, 96.3% and 93.0% respectively; p=0.11), and Sanya Station residents were the most likely of the three to give Swahili as their preferred language (87.4% versus 79.2% and 49.0%; p<0.001), so any language disadvantage would work against the better performance observed there.

text.text: We emphasise that the ladder captures self-rated position rather than explicit comparison with a specified reference group, so this interpretation remains hypothesisgenerating.

It nonetheless converges with evidence that structural inequality shapes brain outcomes beyond individual characteristics, including multi-country work in which income inequality predicted brain dynamics more strongly than individual demographic or cognitive factors. 45 An alternative and complementary possibility is that factors operating at individual, social and community level in Sanya Station attenuate the effect of material deprivation.

text.text: Social cohesion, shared cultural identity, intergenerational support, and dietary or activity differences between lowland and highland settings are plausible candidates, but were not measured here. 46, 47 These findings speak to a growing argument that dementia and brain health prevention frameworks must extend beyond individual behaviour change to address structural determinants. 25, 26 Our data are consistent with the argument that the 2024 Lancet Commission framework under-represents the realities of the global south, 23, 24 and extend the small African evidence base, which has linked multidimensional poverty to dementia in South Africa and to depressive symptoms in Kenya, by examining cognition and depression together in the same East African population, a region projected to experience one of the steepest global increases in dementia cases by 2050. 20 That living standards deprivation predicted depression most strongly while educational deprivation predicted cognition most strongly suggests that different dimensions of poverty may call for different responses, and the balance is likely to differ by setting: individual behaviour change may carry most of the preventable fraction where living conditions and health care are already secure, whereas in lower-income settings structural measures such as access to care, housing and food security plausibly come first, with behaviour change adding to rather than substituting for them.

text.text: This study has several strengths, including a large community-based sample with high participation, assessment instruments validated for the local setting, a theoretically grounded deprivation measure, principled handling of missing data, and prespecified sensitivity analyses addressing the main structural concerns with the composite.
Several limitations must be acknowledged.

The cross-sectional design precludes inference about temporal ordering or causal direction, and depression and cognitive impairment may plausibly contribute to deprivation as well as result from it. 18 Deprivation was measured at a single time point, so we cannot distinguish chronic from recently acquired disadvantage, a meaningful limitation given that cumulative life-course disadvantage is central to the conceptual model motivating this work. 3 Both the GDS-15 and the IDEA are screening instruments rather than diagnostic assessments.

text.text: Perceived social standing was measured only as self-rated position on the MacArthur ladder, which does not identify the reference group against which participants compare themselves, so relative deprivation could not be tested directly.

Several index indicators, notably food insecurity and perceived safety, are self-reported as is the depression measure, raising the possibility of common method bias; 49 the convergence of the depression finding with objectively measured cognitive outcomes offers partial reassurance but cannot exclude this.

Several standard global index indicators, including sanitation, drinking water, asset ownership, and child mortality, could not be included because the corresponding data were unavailable, so our index is an adapted rather than complete implementation.

Residential history would help in interpreting the community-level contrast, but the item was administered to only a small subset of participants and almost entirely in one community, so it could not be compared across sites.

Year of birth was not known for a small number of participants, whose age was estimated, and a small number of recorded ages at the extreme upper end of the distribution should be treated as approximate.

One finding remains unexplained: net of deprivation and other covariates, more years of education was associated with modestly higher depressive symptom scores, which runs counter to the typically protective association reported in the literature.
This may reflect heightened awareness of relative disadvantage, differential item interpretation, or residual confounding, and merits dedicated investigation.

Finally, the three communities lie within a single district of one Tanzanian region and were purposively selected as exemplars of highland and lowland, higher and lower socioeconomic status settings, so the community-level inversion we observed is specific to this configuration and should not be assumed to be generalisable without replication.

Different dimensions of deprivation predicted different outcomes, which suggests that anti-poverty interventions targeting brain health may need to be dimension-specific rather than undifferentiated.

The inversion of this relationship at the community level, where the most materially deprived community showed the best outcomes while rating its social position no lower than the least deprived, indicates that absolute deprivation alone cannot explain the distribution of brain health and points toward relative 25 position within a salient reference group, and toward unmeasured resilience factors in the least materially advantaged community, as candidate explanations meriting dedicated study.
These findings support calls to broaden dementia and brain health prevention frameworks beyond individual behaviour change to encompass the structural conditions in which older adults live.
